dwarf-fortress game sourced

Dwarf Fortress

A colony sim in which the player directs a fortress of autonomous dwarves inside a procedurally generated world whose history, geology, fluids, bodies, and minds are all simulated.

2006Bay 12 GamesColony simcluster c0129 mechanics
this record asyaml sourcemarkdownjson

core loop

embark and dig -> designate jobs, stockpiles, and workshops -> dwarves self-assign labors and craft -> needs, emotions, and stress accumulate -> migrants, caravans, sieges, and beasts arrive -> fortress thrives or collapses into the world's legends

design notes

Tarn Adams's stated principles are to break a system into parts, avoid overplanning, and base each model on a real-world analog; he describes the game as a story generator. The fortress is embarked inside a world whose geology and history were already simulated, and the fortress's own events flow back into that history through Legends, so a collapse becomes a record that a later adventurer can visit. Strange moods let an inspired dwarf seize a workshop to make a named artifact and go insane if materials are missing, which turns the production system into a story source. The game was free and donation-funded from 2006; a paid Steam edition with sprite graphics followed in December 2022, still short of a 1.0 version.

29 stored edges
uses

Designation orders

The player designates digging, chopping, construction, and workshop jobs; dwarves with the matching labor enabled pick them up, and a manager can queue work orders automatically.

core
uses

Fluid and gas simulation

Water and magma flow tile by tile with up to seven depth levels per tile, so breaching a river, cavern lake, or magma source floods connected tunnels.

core
uses

History chronicle

Legends mode lists historical figures, sites, artifacts, and civilizations with a historical map; fortress deeds and retired adventurers are added, and the archive exports to XML.

core
uses

Simulated history generation

World generation builds elevation, rainfall, drainage, temperature, and vegetation layers, then simulates civilizations, sites, and historical figures for a player-chosen number of years before the fortress is embarked.

core
uses

Injury body model

Body parts are layered tissues (skin, fat, muscle, bone, nerves) damaged individually in combat; injuries can be permanent and are treated in a hospital with traction benches, casts, sutures, and splints.

core
uses

Mood and breakdowns

Emotions add to or subtract from a hidden stress value (-1,000,000 to +1,000,000) with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000; stressed dwarves throw tantrums, fall into depression, or wander obliviously, prolonged stress leads to insanity, and one breakdown can spread unhappiness.

core
uses

Stress accumulation

Emotions from events add to or subtract from a hidden stress value (-1,000,000 to +1,000,000) scaled by facets such as stress vulnerability and bravery; above +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000 dwarves risk tantrums, depression, obliviousness, and insanity, and long-term memories keep adding stress.

core
uses

Vertical layers

Z-levels, added in 2007, let the fortress descend level by level through soil and stone to caverns, the magma sea, and the underworld, connected by stairs and ramps.

core
uses

Adaptive threat scaling

Wealthier and more populous fortresses attract sieges and megabeasts.

uses

Needs decay

Food, drink, and sleep, plus personal needs such as socializing or praying met at taverns, temples, and libraries.

supporting
uses

Personality traits

Facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale how stress builds and dissipates.

supporting
uses

Production chains

Ore is smelted to bars and alloyed; steel needs flux to make pig iron plus coke or charcoal, and magma can replace fuel.

supporting
uses

Raid defense

Ambushes, sieges, megabeasts, and forgotten beasts are met with squads, fortifications, and traps triggered by levers or pressure plates.

supporting
uses

Relationship values

Friends, family, and pets; their deaths are major stressors.

Furniture defines bedrooms, dining halls, and offices; nobles demand rooms of rising value.
